title: Promise and Letters
premise: Rosalind Galloway has spent ten years answering anonymous letters left in the lighthouse keeper's box, pouring her grief over her grandfather's death and her abandoned writing career into replies she never expected anyone to read. When the letter writer—Elias Thorne, a retired magistrate who once wronged her family in an inheritance dispute—moves into the cottage next door, Rosalind must confront the man behind the words and the mirror of her own complicity in staying silent. As they restore the lighthouse together against a developer's deadline, their slow-burning bond forces both to choose between legal justice and moral repair. In the end, Rosalind signs her first novel with her real name, Elias deeded the lighthouse back to her family, and she forgives herself enough to love in the present tense.
about_author: August Eastwick is the pen name of a former coastal archivist who spent years cataloguing lighthouse logs and letters before turning to fiction. They write quiet romances about people who mistake solitude for safety.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Box
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She tends the decommissioned lighthouse, finds a new letter in the keeper's box—the first in months—and answers it by habit. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for peace; the reader senses her carefully managed isolation cracking open.

chapters.title: A Moving Van at Saltglass Cottage
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A stranger arrives next door: silver-haired, courteous, unsettlingly familiar in his phrasing. He introduces himself as Elias Thorne. Beat: unease beneath politeness; she notices he quotes her own returned letters back to himself like scripture.

chapters.title: Past Tense
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He unpacks boxes of unsent drafts, revealing he has written to Rosalind for a decade under a false name, seeking a forgiveness he doesn't believe he deserves. Beat: guilt braided with longing; his fear of being recognized.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Left
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She reviews the contested will that gave the lighthouse land to a trust controlled by Thorne's old court ruling, not to her family. Beat: old anger resurfacing; she realizes who her neighbor must be.

chapters.title: Tea, Unpoisoned
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Rosalind invites Elias to tea intending confrontation; instead he confesses nothing but listens so well it undoes her. Beat: the first crack of intimacy; she leaves angrier at herself than at him.

chapters.title: The Developer's Letter
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A demolition notice arrives—the lighthouse is scheduled for sale to a resort firm in ninety days. Beat: stakes crystallize; her sanctuary now has an expiration date, mirroring her fear of attachment.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He offers to help fight the sale, hiding that his own inheritance sits entangled with the trust. Beat: self-serving hope tangled with genuine care; he begins choosing her over his secret.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Fault
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The village rallies—her chosen family of fishermen, the postmistress, a teenage runaway named Wren she informally fosters. Beat: warmth and friction; Wren sees through Rosalind's deflections before Rosalind does.

chapters.title: Drafts and Confessions
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He nearly tells Rosalind he wrote the letters; instead he reads one aloud as 'a stranger's words,' watching her soften. Beat: exquisite dishonesty; love built on a withheld truth.

chapters.title: Storm Damage
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A storm floods the cottage; Elias shelters her and Wren. Working side by side repairing the lighthouse lamp, something wordless passes between them. Beat: tenderness under pressure; the almost-kiss interrupted by Wren.

chapters.title: The Trustee's Terms
chapters.summary: Dual POV. They meet the trustee: the sale can be blocked only if a Galloway heir files a claim within sixty days—but the paperwork requires proof Rosalind's grandfather intended her to inherit. Beat: hope with a hook; the past becomes evidence.

chapters.title: Letters as Evidence
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Searching the archive, she discovers her grandfather's final letter was never delivered—intercepted decades ago by the court. Beat: betrayal deepens; the injustice was systemic, and Elias's name is on the order.

chapters.title: The Man in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Rosalind finds the court order bearing his signature and confronts him. He admits everything except the letters. Beat: rupture; her fury is doubled because she'd begun to love him.

chapters.title: Silence, Answered
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She stops answering the anonymous letters, then rereads ten years of them and recognizes Elias's handwriting in the margins of her own life. Beat: devastating clarity; the person she trusted most was the person she most needed to forgive.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Wren's POV (first time). The runaway asks Rosalind why staying invisible feels safer than being loved, forcing Rosalind to hear her own logic spoken aloud. Beat: mirror moment; Rosalind sees that forgiving Elias requires forgiving herself first.

chapters.title: The Undelivered Letter
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He tracks down the retired clerk who intercepted the grandfather's letter and obtains a sworn statement—at cost to his remaining reputation. Beat: redemption through action; justice pursued outside the law that failed them.

chapters.title: Deadline Day
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the trustee hearing, Elias publicly confesses his role in the original ruling and presents the clerk's affidavit. The claim proceeds. Beat: climax of justice; he sacrifices his name to restore hers.

chapters.title: What I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He leaves the full decade of letters on her doorstep and walks away, asking nothing. Reading them, Rosalind weeps—not for the deception but for the decade they both spent unworthy of each other. Beat: emotional climax; grief transmuted into understanding.

chapters.title: Forgiveness, Present Tense
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She writes him one final letter and delivers it by hand to Saltglass Cottage—an answer, not a verdict. Beat: reversal of their entire dynamic; she chooses visibility over safety.

chapters.title: Deed and Dawn
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The lighthouse is formally restored to Rosalind; Elias signs over his inherited stake without condition. They relight the lamp together at dawn. Beat: resolution of inheritance theme; two broken legacies made whole.

chapters.title: Bylines
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She finishes her novel and submits it under her real name, dedicating it to 'the man who wrote first.' Wren officially stays. Beat: found family sealed; her voice reclaimed from the past tense.

chapters.title: The First Letter of the Rest
chapters.summary: Dual POV closing chapter. Months later, a new letter appears in the keeper's box—signed this time, from Elias, asking her to dinner. She answers in person. Beat: full-circle ending; love no longer deferred, the light kept burning.
